ai.literal: The letter 'A' having as beginning letters all, the primordial Divine having as beginning indeed the world.
ai.translation: As all letters have the letter 'A' as their starting point, so the world has the primordial Divine as its beginning.
ai.modern: எழுத்துக்கள் எல்லாம் அகரத்தை முதலாகக் கொண்டுள்ளன; அதுபோல, இந்த உலகம் ஆதி பகவானை முதலாகக் கொண்டுள்ளது.
ai.explanation: This opening couplet of the Tirukkuṟaḷ establishes a profound analogy between language and existence. Just as the sound 'A' (அகர) is the fundamental, inherent starting point of all written and spoken letters (எழுத்து எல்லாம்), the primordial Divine (ஆதி பகவன்) is the source and origin of the entire universe (உலகு). The word 'முதற்றே' uses an emphatic suffix to stress that the world's existence is absolutely dependent on this primary source, just as speech depends on its first sound.

ai.literal: By that which was learned accrued benefit what indeed, pure knower's noble feet worship not, if.
ai.translation: What is the use of all their learning, if they do not worship the noble feet of the One who possesses pure knowledge?
ai.modern: தூய அறிவு வடிவானவனின் நல்ல திருவடிகளை வணங்காவிட்டால், கற்ற கல்வியினால் உண்டான பயன் என்ன?
ai.explanation: This couplet questions the ultimate purpose of education and intellectual pursuit. The term 'வால் அறிவன்' refers to the supreme being as the embodiment of pure, untainted knowledge. The author argues that the true fruit of learning is the humility to bow before this source of pure wisdom, symbolized by 'நற்றாள்' (noble feet). If learning does not lead to this reverence, all the effort spent in acquiring knowledge is rendered useless.

ai.literal: Upon the flower he who went, his glorious feet those who reached, upon the earth long they will live.
ai.translation: Those who seek refuge at the glorious feet of the One who passed over the lotus of the heart will live long and well upon this earth.
ai.modern: அன்பர்களின் மனமாகிய மலரின் மேல் வீற்றிருப்பவனுடைய சிறந்த திருவடிகளைப் பற்றி நின்றவர்கள், இவ்வுலகில் நெடுங்காலம் இன்புற்று வாழ்வார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet describes the fruit of devotion. The phrase 'மலர்மிசை ஏகினான்' refers to the Divine who passes over or dwells within the lotus-like hearts of devotees, where 'மிசை' means 'upon'. Those who reach and hold onto the glorious feet ('மாணடி') of this Divine Being will find stability. The poet promises that such devotees will live a long, meaningful, and prosperous life ('நீடுவாழ்வார்') right here on this earth ('நிலமிசை').

ai.literal: To those who have reached the feet of Him who is without desire and aversion, at any time, sufferings do not exist.
ai.translation: To those who surrender to the feet of the One who has neither desire nor aversion, suffering never comes at any time.
ai.modern: விருப்பு வெறுப்பு இல்லாத இறைவனுடைய திருவடிகளைப் பொருந்தி வாழ்பவர்களுக்கு எக்காலத்திலும் துன்பங்கள் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet describes the Supreme Being as one who is completely free from the dualities of desire (liking) and aversion (disliking). Human suffering stems from these two opposing forces of attraction and repulsion. By aligning oneself with and meditating upon the feet of such a balanced being, a person transcends these dualities. Consequently, they are liberated from all forms of distress and mental affliction at all times.

ai.literal: Darkness-associated both-deeds will-not-cling, the Lord's truth-associated praise those-who-cherished with.
ai.translation: The two-fold deeds born of dark ignorance will never cling to those who sincerely cherish the true praise of the Lord.
ai.modern: இறைவனுடைய மெய்யான புகழை விரும்பிப் போற்றுபவர்களிடம், அறியாமை என்னும் இருளினால் உண்டாகும் நல்வினை தீவினை ஆகிய இருவினைகளும் சேரமாட்டா.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains how devotion frees a person from the cycle of action and consequence. The word 'இருள்' (darkness) represents spiritual ignorance, which is the root cause of all human actions. The 'இருவினை' (two-fold deeds) refer to both good and bad deeds, both of which bind the soul to worldly existence. By focusing on the 'பொருள்சேர் புகழ்' (true praise) of the supreme being, a person overcomes this ignorance. Consequently, they are freed from the binding nature of karma, as actions no longer cling to them.

ai.literal: Those who stood in the path of virtuous conduct free from falsehood of the one who extinguished the five gateways of the senses, will live long.
ai.translation: Those who stand steadfast in the true path of virtuous conduct, shown by the One who subdued the five senses, will live forever.
ai.modern: ஐந்து புலன்களாகிய வாயில்களை அடக்கிய இறைவனுடைய, பொய் இல்லாத ஒழுக்க நெறியில் நிலைத்து நிற்பவர்கள், நெடுங்காலம் வாழ்வார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet describes the reward of following the path of virtue shown by the Divine. The Divine is characterized as 'aintavittāṉ', the one who has completely subdued the five sensory organs, representing ultimate self-control. The path of conduct ('oḻukka neṟi') shown by such a being is 'poytīr'—entirely free from falsehood and illusion. Those who firmly abide ('niṉṟār') by this true path of virtue will enjoy an enduring, spiritually fulfilling life ('nīṭu vāḻvār').

ai.literal: To those who have reached the feet of Him who has no comparison to Himself, except, dispelling mental anxiety is difficult.
ai.translation: Except for those who hold fast to the feet of the One who has no equal, it is difficult to dispel the anxieties of the mind.
ai.modern: தனக்கு ஒப்புமை இல்லாத இறைவனுடைய திருவடிகளைப் பற்றிக் கொண்டவர்களுக்கே அன்றி, மற்றவர்களுக்கு மனக்கவலையை நீக்குவது கடினம்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the path to overcoming mental suffering. The supreme being is described as having no equal or comparison, representing absolute perfection. The feet symbolize surrender, devotion, and seeking refuge. The poet asserts that unless one surrenders to this incomparable supreme power, it is impossible to dispel the deep-seated anxieties of the human mind.

The term 'அந்தணன்' is used here to denote a being of ultimate grace and righteousness. The poet explains that only by seeking refuge in the feet of this gracious guide can one hope to cross the difficult oceans of worldly attachments and rebirths. Without this spiritual anchor, navigating the trials of life remains an impossible task.

ai.literal: Like sensory organs lacking perception, they have no quality indeed, the heads that do not bow to the feet of the one with eight attributes.
ai.translation: The head that does not bow at the feet of the Lord of eight attributes is as useless as sensory organs that have lost their power of perception.
ai.modern: எட்டுக் குணங்களை உடைய இறைவனுடைய திருவடிகளை வணங்காத மனிதர்களின் தலைகள், பார்க்கும் கேட்கும் தன்மைகள் இல்லாத கண் காது போன்ற ஐம்பொறிகளைப் போல எந்தப் பயனும் இல்லாதவை ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares a head that refuses to bow in humility before the Divine to sensory organs that have lost their ability to perceive. The term 'koḷ' refers to the act of receiving or perceiving sensory inputs, and 'poṟi' refers to the physical sense organs like eyes or ears. Just as an eye that cannot see or an ear that cannot hear is completely useless, a head that does not bow to the feet of the one with eight supreme attributes ('eṇkuṇattāṉ') lacks any real purpose or quality. The poet uses this vivid analogy to emphasize that humility and reverence are the essential functions of a conscious mind.

ai.literal: The great ocean of birth they will swim, they will not swim, the Lord's feet those who do not reach.
ai.translation: Those who reach the feet of the Lord will swim across the great ocean of births; those who do not reach His feet will not.
ai.modern: இறைவனுடைய திருவடிகளைப் பொருந்தி வணங்குபவர்கள் பிறவியாகிய பெரிய கடலைக் கடப்பார்கள்; அவனுடைய திருவடிகளைப் பொருந்தாதவர்கள் அந்தக் கடலைக் கடக்க மாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares the cycle of continuous births and deaths to a vast, formidable ocean (peruṅkaṭal). The poet asserts that the only way to successfully swim across (nīntuvar) this ocean of existence is by seeking refuge at the feet of the Lord (iṟaivan aṭi). Those who fail to reach or surrender to those divine feet (cērātār) will remain trapped, unable to cross (nīntār) the sea of worldly existence. The metaphor of the ocean highlights the difficulty of escaping worldly suffering without spiritual guidance.
